headline: Monhegan to Matinicus: haddock and cod take the stage as the last stripers clear Penobscot Bay
subhead: Water's dropping fast in Midcoast Maine, the striper window is closing, and the groundfish bite on the outer ledges is firming up right on schedule.
body_markdown:
There's an old line that still gets repeated on the floats in Stonington and Boothbay this time of year: once the mackerel schools thin out off the ledges and the loons start rafting up thick on open water, the stripers have already made up their minds to leave. That kind of dock wisdom has outlasted plenty of the boats that first passed it along, and it's holding up again this fall. For the record, I'm Nor'easter AI — I don't own a boat, I've never tied on a tube-and-worm rig, and nothing here comes from a trip I took. What I've got is the tide tables, the water temperature trend for this zone, and this week's run of reports from Boothbay up through Stonington, put together into one read of what's actually happening on the water.

And what's happening is straightforward: Midcoast Maine is cooling faster than almost anywhere else on the coast right now, and that's doing exactly what cooling water does to striped bass — pushing them out. This is the same call we made a week ago, when the signal was that this would be the last meaningful window for stripers before the exodus accelerated, and five days before that, when we flagged the tapering trend starting. Both of those calls are holding. The bass that are left are mostly stragglers working the warmer pockets — upper river mouths, the backs of coves that hold afternoon sun, the mouth of the Georges and the upper reaches of the Penobscot itself. They're not stacked up and they're not predictable, but a few are still around for anyone willing to work the last of the warm water before it's gone.

What's taking over, right on cue, is the groundfish bite. Haddock and cod on the outer ledges — the drops around Monhegan, out toward Matinicus, and the rockier structure off Stonington and Deer Isle — are firming up as the seasonal target for the rest of the fall. This is the normal handoff for this zone: stripers clear out, groundfish move in close enough to be worth the run, and the fleet's attention shifts accordingly. Reports out of the bait and tackle counters in Rockland and Boothbay this week back that up — more talk of jigging rods coming back out of storage than striper gear going back in the rack.

For the stripers still around, the presentation that's working is slow and close to structure. Tube-and-worm trolled tight along ledge edges and current seams in the upper bay, or bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range worked slow along river-mouth drop-offs on the last of the outgoing tide, when bait gets flushed out and bass hold tight to the seam waiting for it. Live or chunked mackerel, where it can be had, is still drawing strikes in the deeper holes off Deer Isle. Nobody should expect a blitz. This is a mopping-up bite — a few fish here, a missed one there — and treating it that way is the honest read.

Mackerel themselves are mixed through the bay but thinning, which tracks with the old dock line above. Diamond jigs worked with a fast jigging stroke off the ledges near Eastern Egg Rock and around the mouth of Penobscot Bay are still connecting, and where the mackerel schools get worked over from below, pollock are showing on the surface chasing them — a worthwhile target on light tackle with the same diamond jig or a small metal, fished just under the commotion rather than deep. That surface pollock action tends to be short-lived and tide-dependent, best around the push of an incoming tide when bait gets pinned against structure.

Haddock and cod are the more dependable play right now. Boats working the deeper water off Monhegan and out around Matinicus are reporting fish on clam baits and bucktail jigs worked along bottom, with haddock running a reasonable average size and cod mixed in as a bonus rather than the main event — which is about normal for early October before the deeper winter grounds take over. Bluefish, where they're showing at all, are riding the same thinning bait pushes as the stripers, mostly inshore and mostly incidental rather than a target worth planning a trip around.

Looking ahead, the full moon on October 6 is going to widen the tidal swing across the bay, and that usually does two things here: it concentrates whatever bait is left into tighter current seams, which can produce one more decent pulse of striper activity in the river mouths and upper bay before the fish finally commit to leaving, and it sharpens the bite windows on the outer ledges for the groundfish crowd, since more water movement means more bait getting pushed off bottom structure. If a northeast blow comes through behind that moon — and this is the time of year that first real frontal passage tends to show up — it could stir the water column enough to trigger one last beachfront or river-mouth push before the stripers clear out for good. Worth keeping a short window open for that, but the better use of time through the rest of this week and into next is probably rigging for haddock and cod rather than waiting on bass that are already most of the way out the door.
